chapter: Los Angeles, Central Avenue and the Apex
title: How Central Avenue became all black
summary: Willard and Royal discuss the mixed Jewish and black population of the East Side and how wartime migration made it a black ghetto for economic reasons.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I have heard that you (inaudible) southeast Los Angeles was a racial mix and Central Avenue was also. In fact, there were as much or as many Jewish people there as there were black people.
That was told to me by the man who, I think, owns the Dunbar now.
The son of the original owner --
-- of that property down there. I think it was Bluestone. At what point did it become all black? When I first knew it, it was just about all black.

Well, this -- the real change came probably after World War II or just about that time because so many people were brought into work in defense factories and things like that during World War I, from the time 1940, '41, before we actually got into the actual fracas of the World War II as one of the allies, they were importing people from the South and most of those people were people that were getting menial jobs and jobs that took no college education and other things as that, so going along with their line of living and the amount of money that they made, they had to find places where they could stay.

So they started getting into the older neighborhoods of the cities and when they came into the run-down sections, they all surrounded each other and looked up and it was a whole black ghetto, strictly an economic situation. They went where they could afford to rent and you rented in the older parts of town. The East Side happened to be one of the older parts of town.
